land.text: the Savoyard mainland and, from the exchange for Sicily, the island of Sardinia

predecessors.note: The same Savoyard state under a new royal title: 'The term Kingdom of Sardinia denotes the Savoyard state from 1720 to 1861' and the exchange 'was formally ratified in the Treaty of The Hague of 17 February 1720'. The dossier starts in 1721 because the house-of-savoy dossier draws 1720 and Cliopatria's row begins in 1721.

land.text: the Sardinian state with Lombardy, central Italy, the Two Sicilies, Marche and Umbria, as the kingdom of Italy drew it from 1861

successors.note: 'On 17 March 1861, law no. 4671 of the Parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy'; the Italian dossier's first keyframe reuses the 1862 outline for 1861.

capitals.name: Turin
capitals.note: 'it was the Piedmontese city of Turin ... which was the de facto seat of power'; Cagliari stayed the capital of the island and its viceroys 'by law'.

capitals.name: Cagliari
capitals.note: The court lived on the island of Sardinia in exile 'from 1798 to 1814' (Charles Emmanuel IV left after the French forced him to abdicate on 6 December 1798); Victor Emmanuel I was in Cagliari in 1802 (Subalpine Republic page).

capitals.name: Turin
capitals.note: 'The seat of government was moved in 1865 from Turin, the old Sardinian capital, to Florence' (the Kingdom of Italy's capital move, after this state's end).

keyframe_review.note: 72,009 km2, 1721-1733: the mainland of the house-of-savoy 1720 shape with the island of Sardinia (84 cells). The page gives no infobox area, so no ratio could be taken. Its 'from 1720' (Treaty of The Hague, 17 February 1720) is drawn by house-of-savoy_1720; Cliopatria's row starts in 1721.

correction.text: the 1721 shape for 1734-1737: the Milanese land held by Franco-Sardinian troops is occupied Austrian land, hatched by the ledger, not Sardinian territory

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria adds 28 cells (78,399 km2; cells around Pavia, Lake Maggiore and the Novarese, lon 6.9-9.4 E) for 1734-1737. The page: 'French and Savoyard troops numbering over 50,000, under the command of Charles Emmanuel, entered Milanese territory' (October 1733) and Milan surrendered by 3 November; the land was ceded only in the Treaty of Vienna, November 1738 ('A preliminary peace was finally concluded in October 1735'). Occupation before cession is hatched, not drawn as territory (rule 4).

74,023 km2. Treaty of Vienna, November 1738: 'Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia received territories in the western part of the Duchy of Milan west of the Ticino, including Novara and Tortona.' The 10 cells added over the 1721 shape (Novarese) agree; Cliopatria drops the rest of the 1734 conquest. The page does not name the Oltrepo Pavese. Repair: the 1738 shape holds only to 1742; the Milanese cells Cliopatria adds in 1748 were ceded at Worms on 13 September 1743 (War of the Austrian Succession page; habsburg-monarchy /ledger/86), see kingdom-of-sardinia_1743.

correction.text: unchanged, but only for 1738-1742: from 1743 the new keyframe kingdom-of-sardinia_1743 applies
the 1748 shape from 1743: 'the Austrians ceded all their territories west of the river Ticino and Lake Maggiore, along with lands south of the Po' (Treaty of Worms, 13 September 1743)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (eu-13-j repair of the reviewer's finding): Cliopatria draws the 17 cells of the Worms cession only from 1748 (the Aix-la-Chapelle page lists the cession again); habsburg-monarchy dates the loss to 13 September 1743. The Franco-Spanish captures of Villefranche (April 1744) and of Alessandria, Valenza and Casale (September 1745) stay in the shape and are hatched by the ledger. The page names no town; Piacenza, named at Worms in other accounts, is not on the page and went to Parma in 1748 ('gaining the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza for Infante Philip').

77,675 km2, 1748-1791: 17 cells (lon 6.9-9.2 E, lat 44.7-46.3 N) added. Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, 18 October 1748: 'Austria cedes minor territories in Italy to Sardinia, including' Vigevano; the page is silent on the Oltrepo Pavese and Anghiera, which the added cells appear to cover, and on the Treaty of Worms (1743). Repair: the 17 cells are Sardinian from 13 September 1743 in this dossier (kingdom-of-sardinia_1743; War of the Austrian Succession page); this shape is right from 1748. Infobox area: page silent.

correction.text: without Savoy, which the page says 'had been annexed by France in 1792'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria keeps Savoy (45 of 46 cells) in the 1792-1793 shape and drops it only in 1794; the page dates the French annexation to 1792. The County of Nice page (reopened in the eu-13-j repair) has the French entering Nice on 29 September 1792 and the Convention ordering its integration into France on 31 January (1793); Sardinia ceded it formally by the Treaty of Paris, 15 May 1796, so Nice stays in the shape and is hatched as occupied (ledger).

correction.text: without the Savoy cells (10 of 46) that remain in Cliopatria's 1794 shape: Savoy was French from 1792

keyframe_review.note: 62,118 km2 for 1794-1795 after the drop of 63 cells; Nice (4 of 17 cells) is still there and goes in 1796 (Treaty of Paris). Savoy was annexed in 1792 on the page.

correction.text: Piedmont, Aosta and the island, without Savoy and Nice, ceded by the Treaty of Paris of 15 May 1796; the fortress districts of Alessandria, Coni and Tortona stay in the shape, held by France in occupation

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria drops 45 more cells (Alessandria, Cuneo and Tortona districts, 50,928 km2). Armistice of Cherasco, 28 April 1796: Sardinia 'handed over Alessandria, Coni and Tortone to Republican France'; Treaty of Paris, 15 May 1796: 'the county of Nice, the duchy of Savoy, Tende and Beuil to France'. Occupied is not lost, so the districts stay and are hatched; Nice and Savoy are lost.

correction.text: Piedmont, Aosta and the island, without Savoy and Nice; from December 1798 the mainland is under French occupation (hatched)

keyframe_review.note: 55,532 km2 for 1797-1799: Cliopatria restores 21 of the 45 dropped cells in 1797; no page opened explains that. The king 'was forced ... to abdicate and leave for the island of Sardinia' on 6 December 1798 (Kingdom of Sardinia page) and the Piedmontese Republic was in place in 1798-99 (Subalpine Republic page), so the mainland is occupied land in 1798-1799, not an independent shape.

correction.text: for 1800-1801 only: Piedmont and Aosta under French occupation (hatched) with the island; from 1802 the mainland is French and Italian-Republic land, see kingdom-of-sardinia_1802

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria draws 62,118 km2 (Piedmont, Aosta, Sardinia) up to 1813, the same outline as 1794. The Subalpine Republic page: the republic 'was divided between the French Republic and the Italian Republic' on 11 September 1802; Charles Emmanuel IV abdicated on 4 June 1802 in favour of Victor Emmanuel I, who was in Cagliari. A king who ruled only the island cannot be drawn with Piedmont for 1802-1813.

correction.text: the island of Sardinia, the only land the Savoyard crown held in 1802-1813: the court lived there 'from 1798 to 1814'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1802-1813 (84 gazetteer cells, about 21,200 km2), replacing Cliopatria's 62,118 km2 outline: on 11 September 1802 the Subalpine Republic's departements went to France and Novara to the Italian Republic (Subalpine Republic page). Victor Emmanuel I (1802-1821, Kingdom of Sardinia page) reigned from Cagliari.

minus.text: the part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery

correction.text: with Liguria ('In 1814, the Crown of Savoy enlarged its territories with the addition of the former Republic of Genoa') and without the part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery, which the First Treaty of Paris left to France

keyframe_review.note: 74,357 km2: Piedmont's western part, Aosta, Savoy and Nice and the island come back in 1814, but Cliopatria leaves Liguria out until 1815 although the page dates the addition of Genoa to 1814 ('returned to Savoy its peninsular possessions and augmented them with Liguria', Congress of Vienna 1814-1815). The Savoy and Nice return is not dated on this page (confidence 1 in the ledger). Repair: the Treaty of Paris (1814) page has France 'allowed to retain' 'part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery' (30 May 1814); that part (two 25 km discs, 15 cells, my placement) is removed for 1814 and returns in 1815 (ledger, confidence 1).

78,009 km2, 1815-1847: Liguria (15 of 24 cells) in; nine Piedmontese cells beyond the 1814 shape (on the Novara-Ossola side) are not explained by a page opened, though the Subalpine Republic page has Novara going to the Italian Republic in 1802. Carouge goes to Geneva in 1816 and Monaco becomes a protectorate in 1817 (ledger). Infobox area: page silent. Repair: the Congress of Vienna page (reopened) is silent on Chambery and Annecy, Carouge and the Novara-side cells, so the nine cells stay unexplained; the shape has Savoy whole, consistent with the 1815 return of the Annecy-Chambery part (ledger).

134,622 km2 for 1848 alone: a high-water mark with Lombardy, Veneto and Parma in it, which the ledger dates month by month: Parma 'in the spring', Lombardy 8 June, Venetia 5 July, all lost to the Salasco armistice of 9 August 1848 ('Charles Albert's troops would withdraw'). Use the ledger for the months; the shape is not the year-end state.

77,961 km2: back to the 1815 outline after Novara (23 March 1849). 'Return to the status quo ante bellum' (infobox). Austria held Lomellina and Alessandria in occupation after the Armistice of Vignale (24 March 1849) until the final peace (Treaty of Milan, 6 August 1849); the ledger hatches that.

Unverified: the Congress of Vienna page, reopened in the eu-13-j repair, is silent on any Sardinian change from 1815 to 1860. A one-cell change (lon 7.2 E, lat 43.7 N, at the French frontier near Menton) that no page opened explains. 78,056 km2 for 1853-1858.

correction.text: Piedmont, Liguria, Sardinia and Lombardy: Tuscany and the Emilian duchies only joined on 22 March 1860

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1859 shape (122,175 km2) already holds Tuscany (80 of 86 cells). The page: Sardinia 'later occupied and annexed the United Provinces of Central Italy' and the Papal Legations 'on 22 March 1860'. Lombardy (except Mantua and Legnago) came with the Villafranca settlement of 12 July 1859 (Second Italian War of Independence page; Treaty of Zurich 11 November 1859).

163,326 km2: Sardinia without Savoy and Nice (ceded by the Treaty of Turin, 24 March 1860), with Lombardy, central Italy, Sicily (74 of 89 cells) and part of the mainland south (46 of 262 cells of the gazetteer's Kingdom of Naples region, around 39.5 N). A mid-year composite: the pages date the Two Sicilies' annexation to the plebiscite of 21 October 1860 and Marche and Umbria to November 1860, so the south and the Marche are added by the ledger at those months.

235,522 km2: the same outline the kingdom-of-italy dossier reuses for 1861. The Kingdom of Sardinia ends on 17 March 1861 ('law no. 4671 ... proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy'); the shape stands for the months before the proclamation. Gaeta fell on 13 February 1861 (Expedition of the Thousand page). Infobox area: page silent.

ledger.note: 1721: the Savoyard state continues as the Kingdom of Sardinia. 'The term Kingdom of Sardinia denotes the Savoyard state from 1720 to 1861'; the exchange of Sicily for Sardinia 'was formally ratified in the Treaty of The Hague of 17 February 1720', but 'Until 1723, he continued to style himself King of Sicily rather than King of Sardinia'. The map draws the state from 1721 (Cliopatria's first year); 1720 is in house-of-savoy.

region.text: the Savoyard mainland and the island of Sardinia

ledger.note: October 1733: Franco-Sardinian troops enter the Duchy of Milan. 'French and Savoyard troops numbering over 50,000, under the command of Charles Emmanuel, entered Milanese territory'; 'By 3 November, the city of Milan itself had surrendered.' Sardinia is the occupier, Austria the owner. The region is the 28 cells Cliopatria adds in 1734; the page does not say how much of Milan the Sardinian army held.

region.text: Milanese territory held by Franco-Sardinian troops, 1733-1738 (the cells Cliopatria adds in 1734)

ledger.note: 1738: the occupation of Milanese land ends with the peace. 'A preliminary peace was finally concluded in October 1735 and ratified in the Treaty of Vienna in November 1738.' Cliopatria drops 19 of the cells in 1738.

region.text: Milanese territory held by Franco-Sardinian troops, 1733-1738

ledger.note: 1738: the Treaty of Vienna gives Sardinia Novara and Tortona. 'Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia received territories in the western part of the Duchy of Milan west of the Ticino, including Novara and Tortona.' The region is the cells Cliopatria's 1738 shape adds to the 1721 one; the page is silent on the Oltrepo Pavese.

region.text: the western part of the Duchy of Milan west of the Ticino, including Novara and Tortona

ledger.note: 13 September 1743: the Treaty of Worms cedes the Milanese west of the Ticino. War of the Austrian Succession page: at Worms 'the Austrians ceded all their territories west of the river Ticino and Lake Maggiore, along with lands south of the Po' (the page gives the day; the year is in a link title). habsburg-monarchy /ledger/86 dates the cession to Worms, 13 September 1743, at confidence 3, and the Lomellina page has the Vigevano area 'acquired by Piedmont in 1743'. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle page (18 October 1748) has 'Austria cedes minor territories in Italy to Sardinia, including' Vigevano, which confirms the cession; the Aix page is silent on Worms and the Worms-page extraction names no town. The region is the 17 cells Cliopatria adds only in 1748, my reading. Sardinian possession was interrupted by the Franco-Spanish captures of 1745 (own entries). Reviewer fix: re-dated from 1748 to 1743 (Cliopatria and the first version followed the Aix-la-Chapelle page).

region.text: the Milanese territories west of the Ticino and Lake Maggiore, ceded at Worms: the 17 cells Cliopatria adds in 1748 (including Vigevano)

ledger.note: April 1744: Franco-Spanish troops take Villefranche. War of the Austrian Succession page: 'Gallispan troops under Conti captured Villefranche in April 1744'; 'the Spanish ... captured the important port of Villefranche-sur-Mer, then part of Savoy'. The page does not mention the County of Nice or the Spanish occupation of Savoy from 1742 (a gap), and does not say when the port was returned; the end is bridged to the peace (confidence 1, next entries).

September 1745: the Franco-Spanish army takes Alessandria, Valenza and Casale. War of the Austrian Succession page: it 'defeated the Sardinians at Bassignano on 27 September, then captured Alessandria, Valenza and Casale Monferrato'. Spain is the counterpart because the army is called Franco-Spanish ('Gallispan'); France shared it. The page does not say when the towns came back (it says only that the Austrians took Milan in March 1746 and were driven out of Genoa in December 1746); the end is bridged to the peace. The three discs are my placement; Alessandria is not in the gazetteer as a city.

18 October 1748: the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle ends the war ('on 18 October 1748, the war ended with the signing of the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle'). Bridging entry: the page does not say when the Franco-Spanish forces left Villefranche, and the towns of 1745 may have been recovered earlier (confidence 1).

18 October 1748: the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle ends the war. Bridging entry: the page is silent on the recovery of Alessandria, Valenza and Casale (the Austro-Sardinian advance of 1746 is not described on it), so the true end may be 1746 (confidence 1).

1767-1769: Charles Emmanuel III annexes the Maddalena archipelago. 'In 1767-1769, Charles Emmanuel III annexed the Maddalena archipelago.' The page does not say whose it was; the Corsican Republic (to 1768) and Genoa lie to the north, so the counterpart is left as nobody. A 25 km disc round La Maddalena (not in the gazetteer; the islands are too small for a land cell, so the disc reaches the Gallura coast).
1792: France annexes Savoy. The page says Savoy 'had been annexed by France in 1792'; the war and the month are not on the page. Nice is not dated before the treaty of 1796.

29 September 1792: French troops enter Nice. County of Nice page: the Army of the Midi, 'under the command of General Jacques Bernard d'Anselme, entered the city on 29 September 1792'; 'The following 31 January, the National Convention ordered the integration of the county into French territory' (the page does not print the year, 1793, but it follows from the sequence). Sardinia ceded the county only by the Treaty of Paris of 15 May 1796 (entry below), so the county is kept in the shape and hatched as occupied, as with the Savoyard cells of the 1796 armistice. The region is read as the Alpes-Maritimes departement, as in the 1796 entry. Thin-item fix: occupation of Nice from 1792 added.

April 1796: Napoleon's armistice puts French garrisons in three fortress districts. Armistice of Cherasco, 28 April 1796: Sardinia 'handed over Alessandria, Coni and Tortone to Republican France'. France is the occupier. The region is the 45 cells Cliopatria drops in 1796 (the districts round the three towns), larger than the fortresses themselves.

region.text: Alessandria, Coni (Cuneo) and Tortona with their districts

ledger.note: 15 May 1796: the Treaty of Paris turns the occupation of Nice into a cession ('the county of Nice, the duchy of Savoy, Tende and Beuil' to France; next entry). The counterpart is french-first-republic to pair with the 1792 start: the Directory that signs is the Republic's government from 1795 (Cliopatria and eu-20 give it its own row).

15 May 1796: the Treaty of Paris cedes Nice to France. 'the county of Nice, the duchy of Savoy, Tende and Beuil' go to France (Savoy had been annexed in 1792 and is recorded there); Sardinia also guaranteed free passage for French troops. The region is read as the Alpes-Maritimes departement.

region.text: the county of Nice, Tende and Beuil

ledger.note: December 1798: the fortress districts of 1796 merge into the occupation of all Piedmont. Bridging entry: the pages opened do not say when, or whether, the districts were returned (Cliopatria restores 21 of the 45 cells in 1797). Repair: the Piedmontese Republic page (reopened) has 'General Joubert occupied the capital of Turin on 6 December 1798', 'The Piedmontese Republic was declared on 9 December 1798' and 'France decided to annex Piedmont in February 1799'; it is silent on what became of the fortress districts, so this entry stays a bridge (confidence 1).

region.text: Alessandria, Coni (Cuneo) and Tortona with their districts

ledger.note: December 1798: the court leaves Turin for Cagliari. The French 'forced Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate and leave for the island of Sardinia' on 6 December 1798; the king 'temporarily resided on the island ... from 1798 to 1814'. The Subalpine Republic page has him escaping to Rome; the Kingdom of Sardinia page is followed.

December 1798: France occupies Piedmont. The page: the French 'forced Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate and leave for the island of Sardinia' (6 December 1798); the Piedmontese Republic follows. France is the occupier, the Savoyard crown the owner until the annexation of 1802.

region.text: Piedmont and Aosta, the mainland the crown still claimed

ledger.note: June 1799: Austro-Russian troops end the Piedmontese Republic. The page has it existing 'until 20 June 1799', when 'it was conquered by Austro-Russian troops'. The king did not return.
June 1799: the Austrians hold Piedmont. 'conquered by Austro-Russian troops'; the page names no Austrian administration.

June 1800: Napoleon retakes Piedmont. 'In 1800, Napoleon returned to Italy, taking back much of the new republics'; the Piedmontese Republic 're-established on 20 June 1800'. The page gives no Austrian withdrawal date.
June 1800: France holds Piedmont again, as the Subalpine Republic (1800-1802).
11 September 1802: the Subalpine Republic ends. 'The Subalpine Republic ceased to exist on 11 September 1802, when it was divided between the French Republic and the Italian Republic.'

11 September 1802: Piedmont and Aosta become French departements. 'Doire, Marengo, Pô, Sesia, Stura, and Tanaro went to France'; Charles Emmanuel IV had abdicated on 4 June 1802 and Victor Emmanuel I reigned from Cagliari. Piedmont minus the Novarese.

region.text: the departements Doire, Marengo, Po, Sesia, Stura and Tanaro

ledger.note: 11 September 1802: the Novarese goes to the Italian Republic. 'Novara (as Agogna) went to the Italian Republic.' The Novara province stands for the departement.
1814: the court returns from Cagliari to Turin. The page has the king on the island 'from 1798 to 1814'; Turin is 'the old Sardinian capital' (Unification of Italy page).

1814: Piedmont and Aosta return to the crown. The Congress of Vienna 'returned to Savoy its peninsular possessions and augmented them with Liguria' (1814-1815). The year is Cliopatria's 1814 shape; the region excludes Savoy and Nice, which are a separate entry.

1814: the crown takes Liguria from Genoa. 'In 1814, the Crown of Savoy enlarged its territories with the addition of the former Republic of Genoa, now a duchy'; 'Liguria, taken from the Republic of Genoa' (Congress of Vienna, 1814-1815). Cliopatria draws Liguria from 1815. The page names the donor as the Republic of Genoa; Cliopatria's Ligurian Republic row (ligurian-republic) ends in 1814, so that dossier may carry the matching loss.

region.text: Liguria, taken from the Republic of Genoa

ledger.note: 30 May 1814: Savoy (except the Annecy-Chambery part) and Nice return to the crown. Treaty of Paris (1814) page: 'France's borders of 1 June 1792 were confirmed', which leaves Savoy (annexed in 1792) and Nice (1793) outside France, but France was 'allowed to retain' 'part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery'. The page is silent on Nice and on which part of Savoy was kept; the Congress of Vienna page has the king 're-established in Piedmont, Nice, and Savoy' (Final Act, 9 June 1815). The Annecy-Chambery part is two 25 km discs (15 cells), my placement. Thin-item fix: the entry was a confidence-1 bridge for all of Savoy and Nice.

minus.text: the part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery

region.text: Savoy (except the part with Annecy and Chambery) and Nice

ledger.note: 1815: the Annecy-Chambery part of Savoy comes back. Congress of Vienna page: the King of Sardinia was 're-established in Piedmont, Nice, and Savoy' (Final Act, 9 June 1815). Bridging entry: the Treaty of Paris (1814) page has France keeping the part with Annecy and Chambery, and the Second Treaty of Paris paragraph (20 November 1815) is silent on the Savoy border, so the date of the return is not on any page opened; the reviewer places it in November 1815 (confidence 1). The counterpart is the Bourbon kingdom that signed the treaties of 1814 and 1815, not the Empire of the neighbouring entries.

region.text: the part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery

ledger.note: 1816: Sardinia gives Carouge to Geneva. The Treaty of Turin (1816) 'transferred Carouge and adjacent areas to the newly-created Swiss Canton of Geneva'. The month is not on the page; Carouge is not in the gazetteer (8 km disc south of Geneva).
1817: Sardinia takes Monaco under its protection. 'By the Treaty of Stupinigi (1817), the Kingdom of Sardinia extended its protectorate over the Principality of Monaco.'

Spring 1848: Parma votes to join Sardinia. The page has the duchy of Parma 'voted for annexation by the Kingdom of Sardinia in the spring'; Piacenza, Modena are not on it. Parma province stands for the duchy.
23 March 1848: Sardinia declares war on Austria. 'On 23 March, the Kingdom of Sardinia declared war on the Austrian Empire.' The page dates the declaration, not the first campaign on Lombard ground.

8 June 1848: Lombardy votes for annexation. 'The provisional government of Milan had actually voted in a referendum to accept annexation by Piedmont on 8 June.' The region is Lombardy; Mantua stayed Austrian.

5 July 1848: Venetia votes for annexation. 'the parliament had decided to accept annexation by the Kingdom of Sardinia on 5 July 1848.' Reviewer fix 2026-10-25 (eu-13-j review): the same page has Vicenza retaken by Austria on 11 June and Padua and Treviso on 13 June, and Venice as 'the only city in Lombardy-Venetia which remained in the hands of the insurgents', so the region is narrowed from Veneto to the Venezia province and the confidence lowered to 2.

region.text: Venice, 'the only city in Lombardy-Venetia which remained in the hands of the insurgents'

ledger.note: 9 August 1848: the Salasco armistice gives Lombardy and Venetia back. 'Radetzky and Salasco concluded an armistice which stated that Charles Albert's troops would withdraw.' Custoza was lost on 25 July. The page does not name the lands; Parma is not mentioned.
9 August 1848: the first campaign ends in the Salasco armistice.

August 1848, after the armistice of Salasco (9 August): Parma goes back to its duke. First Italian War of Independence page: 'After the armistice of Salasco, Prince Franz de Paula of Liechtenstein marched on Modena and Parma to restore their deposed dukes.' The page gives no date for the march and does not state its outcome (it says the revolt 'ended in the restoration of traditional institutions'); a brigade of 1849 stands 'opposite Piacenza (in the Duchy of Parma, occupied by the Austrians)'. The month is the armistice's; the region is the one of the spring gain. Reviewer fix: the loss was missing, so the ledger kept Parma Sardinian until 1860.
20 March 1849: the war resumes. 'At noon on 20 March 1849, hostilities officially resumed.' The fighting is on the Ticino, in the Novarese and Lomellina.

23 March 1849: Charles Albert is beaten at Novara. 'The Battle of Novara was the last and bloodiest battle of the First Italian War of Independence'; he abdicated for Victor Emmanuel II the same day, and the Armistice of Vignale followed on 24 March.

24 March 1849: Austria occupies Lomellina and Alessandria. By the Armistice of Vignale 'a force of 20,000 men would remain in Lomellina' and Alessandria was to be occupied until a final peace. Austria is the occupier. Discs of 25 and 20 km stand for the two districts.

6 August 1849: the Treaty of Milan ends the occupation. The page says the Alessandria occupation was 'temporary, pending a final peace'; at Milan 'Piedmont-Sardinia was forced to pay an indemnity of 65 million francs to Austria'. The page does not date the withdrawal.
26 April 1859: war with Austria over Lombardy. 'Upon Sardinia's refusal, the war began on 26 April.' The first battle named is Magenta, 4 June.

12 July 1859: the Armistice of Villafranca ends the fighting. 'The two emperors met on 11 July at Villafranca di Verona and the armistice was signed on the following day'; Solferino, 24 June, 'resulted in the end of the war'.

1859: Lombardy joins Sardinia. 'Austria ceded Lombardy to France, which, in turn, gave it to Sardinia', excluding 'the Austrian fortresses of Mantua and Legnago and the surrounding territory'; Villafranca, 12 July, settled it and the Treaty of Zurich confirmed it on 11 November (Unification of Italy page: 'The settlement, by which Lombardy was annexed to Sardinia, left Austria in control of the Veneto and Mantua').

22 March 1860: the central Italian provinces are annexed. Sardinia 'later occupied and annexed the United Provinces of Central Italy' and the Papal Legations 'on 22 March 1860'. The region is Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna; the page names Tuscany, Parma, Modena and part of the Papal States. The union has no dossier of its own.

region.text: Tuscany, Parma, Modena and the Papal Legations

ledger.note: 24 March 1860: Savoy and Nice go to France. 'Sardinia handed Savoy and Nice over to France at the Treaty of Turin, a decision that was the consequence of the Plombieres Agreement, on 24 March 1860.' Referendums showed over 99.5% in favour (Kingdom of Sardinia page).

1860: the Sardinian protectorate over Monaco ends. Monaco page: 'Monaco remained in this position until 1860 when, by the Treaty of Turin, the Sardinian forces pulled out' and 'Monaco became a French protectorate once again'. The month is that of the Treaty of Turin (24 March 1860, Unification of Italy page). Reviewer fix 2026-10-25 (eu-13-j review): was 1861 at confidence 1 with no page.

11 May 1860: Garibaldi lands at Marsala. 'Garibaldi's landing in Marsala on 11 May 1860'; the Kingdom of Sardinia page has him campaigning 'in the name of the Kingdom of Sardinia'. Calatafimi 15 May, Palermo 27 May, Milazzo 20 July, Calabria 19 August, Naples 7 September, the Volturno 1-2 October. The union covers Sicily and the mainland south.

region.text: Sicily and the mainland south of the Papal States

ledger.note: 11 September 1860: the invasion of the Papal States. 'On 11 September, Cavour instigated the invasion of the Papal States'; the Papal troops were 'besieged in the fortress of Ancona, finally surrendering on 29 September' (Unification of Italy page).
29 September 1860: Ancona surrenders. 'The Piedmontese Army occupied most of Umbria and Marche' after its fall; the page gives no separate date.

21 October 1860: the Two Sicilies vote to join. 'a plebiscite confirmed the annexation of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies to the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia' (1,302,064 votes in the mainland, 432,053 in Sicily); Teano meeting 26 October. The page also has the incorporation on 17 March 1861 and Gaeta holding out to 13 February 1861.

region.text: the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

ledger.note: November 1860: Marche and Umbria vote to join. The page has the two provinces choosing 'to join the Kingdom of Italy by plebiscite' in the month of Victor Emmanuel II's entry into Naples (7 November).
13 February 1861: Gaeta surrenders. The Sardinian army 'concluded the siege on 13 February 1861, defeating the Bourbon army, which surrendered.'

region.text: the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

ledger.note: 17 March 1861: the Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed. 'On 17 March 1861, law no. 4671 of the Parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy.'

region.text: the Savoyard state and the lands it had annexed, as the Kingdom of Italy

wars.name: War of the Polish Succession (Sardinian front)

zones.text: the Duchy of Milan west of the Ticino

wars.outcome: Franco-Sardinian troops entered Milanese territory in October 1733 and held Milan from 3 November; the Treaty of Vienna (November 1738) gave Sardinia the lands west of the Ticino including Novara and Tortona.
wars.note: A preliminary peace was concluded in October 1735. The page names the 'secret Treaty of Turin' of November 1733 between France and Charles Emmanuel.

wars.name: War of the Austrian Succession (Sardinian front)

zones.text: the Milanese territories west of the Ticino ceded at Worms (13 September 1743)

wars.outcome: Treaty of Worms, 13 September 1743: Austria cedes the Milanese west of the Ticino and Lake Maggiore to Sardinia; Franco-Spanish troops take Villefranche (April 1744) and, after Bassignano (27 September 1745), Alessandria, Valenza and Casale; Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, 18 October 1748: Austria cedes minor territories including Vigevano, Sardinia having hoped for Parma.
wars.note: Repair of the reviewer's thin finding: the first version entered only the 1748 settlement. The War of the Austrian Succession page has the Convention of Turin of February 1742 (alliance with Austria), Worms, the capture of Villefranche in April 1744 and the Sardinian defeat at Bassignano in 1745, and is silent on a Spanish occupation of Savoy from 1742, on the County of Nice and on any Sardinian recovery, so those parts of the front are still missing; 1744 is the first campaign the page dates.

wars.name: War of the First Coalition (Sardinian front)
wars.outcome: Savoy annexed by France in 1792; Armistice of Cherasco, 28 April 1796 (Alessandria, Coni, Tortona to France); Treaty of Paris, 15 May 1796: Nice, Savoy, Tende and Beuil ceded and free passage for French troops.
wars.note: The years 1792 (annexation of Savoy) and 1796 are the pages'; the war's other campaigns are not on the pages opened.

wars.name: First Italian War of Independence
wars.outcome: Sardinia declared war on 23 March 1848, annexed Lombardy (8 June) and Venetia (5 July), lost at Custoza (25 July), withdrew by the Salasco armistice (9 August 1848), lost at Novara (23 March 1849); Charles Albert abdicated; Treaty of Milan, 6 August 1849, indemnity of 65 million francs and 'return to the status quo ante bellum'.
wars.note: Austria occupied Lomellina and Alessandria after the Armistice of Vignale (24 March 1849) until the final peace.

wars.name: Second Italian War of Independence
wars.outcome: War from 26 April 1859; Magenta 4 June, Solferino 24 June; Armistice of Villafranca 12 July; Treaty of Zurich 11 November: Austria ceded Lombardy to France, which gave it to Sardinia, except Mantua and Legnago.
wars.note: The page gives Magenta both as 4 and 5 June.

wars.name: Expedition of the Thousand and the annexation of the south
wars.outcome: Garibaldi landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and entered Naples on 7 September; the Piedmontese army invaded the Papal States on 11 September; a plebiscite of 21 October 1860 annexed the Two Sicilies; Gaeta fell on 13 February 1861; the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861.
wars.note: The page gives 17 March 1861 as the incorporation date of the Two Sicilies too; the plebiscite date is followed for the ledger.

certainty.note: Frontiers fixed by treaty: The Hague (17 February 1720), Vienna (November 1738), Aix-la-Chapelle (18 October 1748). The Alpine watershed and the Milanese districts are Cliopatria's cell-scale lines.
Annexations, armistice garrisons and client republics (the Piedmontese and Subalpine republics) make the mainland frontier a matter of occupation; the island is sharp.

Frontiers fixed by treaty: Congress of Vienna (1814-15), Carouge to Geneva (1816), Milan (6 August 1849), Zurich (11 November 1859), Turin (24 March 1860). The southern and Papal annexations of 1860 follow plebiscites, but the new frontier with the Papal Lazio is Cliopatria's line.

notes:
Cliopatria's Kingdom of Sardinia row runs 1721-1861 and is the Savoyard state under the royal title (house-of-savoy before 1721, kingdom-of-italy from 17 March 1861, both with dossiers). The dossier starts in 1721 (Cliopatria's first year; the page says 'from 1720') so as not to overlap house-of-savoy, which draws 1720.
Page budget (9) was spent by the author; the eu-13-j repair of 2026-10-25 opened six more pages because the reviewer's findings needed them (War of the Austrian Succession, Lomellina, County of Nice, Treaty of Paris (1814), Piedmontese Republic, Congress of Vienna) and reopened the First Italian War of Independence page. Still unverified: the nine Piedmontese cells added in 1815 and the one cell of 1853 (the Congress of Vienna page is silent on both); the Spanish occupation of Savoy from 1742 and the County of Nice in 1744-1748 (the War of the Austrian Succession page is silent); the return date of the Annecy-Chambery part of Savoy (the Second Treaty of Paris paragraph is silent); the fate of the 1796 fortress districts (the Piedmontese Republic page is silent). A ruler list was not opened (the pages give Victor Emmanuel I 1802-1821, Charles Felix 1821-1831, Charles Albert 1831-1849 only, so no ruler strip is written).
Cliopatria errors found: the 1800 shape draws Piedmont as Sardinian until 1813 although the crown ruled only the island from 1798 (new keyframe kingdom-of-sardinia_1802 for 1802-1813; 1800-1801 kept as French-occupied Piedmont); Savoy is dropped in 1794 but annexed in 1792 on the page; Tuscany is Sardinian in the 1859 shape but joined on 22 March 1860; the 1860-1861 split of the south and the Marche does not match the plebiscites of 21 October and November 1860; the 1734 shape draws the occupied Milanese land as territory; the 17 Milanese cells of the Worms cession are drawn from 1748, not 1743 (new keyframe kingdom-of-sardinia_1743); the 1814 shape returns all of Savoy although France kept the Annecy-Chambery part.
Eu-13-j repair of 2026-10-25 (reviewer's findings): (1) the Venetian vote of 5 July 1848 covers only Venice (reviewer's edit); (2) the Monaco protectorate ends in March 1860 (reviewer's edit); (3) Parma is lost again after the Salasco armistice (August 1848; First Italian War of Independence page, Liechtenstein's march on Parma and Modena); (4) the Milanese cession west of the Ticino is dated 13 September 1743 (Worms; War of the Austrian Succession page and the Lomellina page for Vigevano) instead of 1748 (Aix-la-Chapelle), with a new keyframe 1743-1747 and the 1738 shape limited to 1738-1742; (5) thin items: Nice occupied from 29 September 1792 (County of Nice page), Franco-Spanish captures of Villefranche (April 1744) and of Alessandria, Valenza and Casale (September 1745) added with bridged ends at the peace, and the 1814 return of Savoy and Nice split into the part France let go (30 May 1814, Treaty of Paris (1814) page) and the Annecy-Chambery part (1815, bridged).
Disagreements with the reviewer: (a) the reviewer says the First Treaty of Paris left Chambery and Annecy French 'until November 1815'; the Treaty of Paris (1814) page I opened says only that France was allowed to retain part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambery and is silent on the Second Treaty's effect on the border, so the return is dated 1815 at confidence 1, with the reviewer's November noted; (b) the reviewer wrote that the war ran 1742-1748 with Spanish occupation of Savoy from 1742; the War of the Austrian Succession page has neither, so the war starts in 1744 (the first campaign it dates) and the 1742 occupation is left as a gap; (c) the Worms cession is entered as one gain of the 17 cells Cliopatria adds in 1748, an approximation the pages cannot refine (they name no town but Vigevano).
Pages disagree: referendums of central Italy on 5 March 1860 (Kingdom of Sardinia page) against annexation on 22 March 1860 (Unification of Italy page; followed); the Subalpine Republic page gives 10 September 1798 for the Piedmontese Republic, the Piedmontese Republic page 9 December 1798 (followed, with the abdication of 6 December 1798 from the Kingdom of Sardinia page) and a French annexation decision of February 1799; the Subalpine Republic page has Charles Emmanuel IV going to Rome, the Kingdom of Sardinia page the exile in Sardinia (the latter followed); the Expedition of the Thousand page has the Two Sicilies incorporated on 17 March 1861 as well as annexed by the plebiscite of 21 October 1860 (the latter followed).
For other batches: habsburg-monarchy (eu-09) has no mirror for the 1733-1738 Franco-Sardinian occupation, the 1738 loss of Novara and Tortona, or the 1799-1800 occupation of Piedmont; duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza, austrian-empire, french-first-republic, french-directory, french-consulate, first-french-empire, second-french-empire, kingdom-of-spain (the 1744-1748 occupations) and united-provinces-of-central-italy have no dossier yet or no mirror. Counterparts needing dossiers: united-provinces-of-central-italy (Tuscany, Parma, Modena and the Legations, 1859-1860; eu-20 or eu-13-x). Gazetteer names needed: La Maddalena, Carouge, Gaeta, Lomellina, Alessandria (city), Villefranche-sur-Mer, Annecy, Chambery (all discs here). Wikipedia gives the Kingdom of Italy's capital move in 1865; that belongs to the kingdom-of-italy dossier. The Perfect Fusion of 1847 (composite to unitary state) changes no border and has no entry.
